nodes.name: Proposition 3.3 (centre of the UHF-part of the amalgamated representation)
nodes.statement:
Let $\omega,\psi$ be as in Proposition 3.2 with Popescu system $({\mathcal K},{\mathcal M},$ $v_k,\Omega)$ be 
taken as in Proposition 2.4 i.e. on support projection. Then the centre of 
$\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is completely atomic and the element 
$E_0=[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)' \vee \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes 
\mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega]$ is a minimal projection in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ and the centre is invariant for both $\Lambda$ and $\tilde{\Lambda}$. Furthermore the 
following holds:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (a) The centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ has the following two disjoint
possibilities:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (i) There exists a positive integer $m \ge 1$ such that the centre is generated by the family of minimal
orthogonal projections $\{ \Lambda_k(E_0): 0 \le k \le m-1 \}$ where $m \ge 1$ is the least positive integer so that
$\Lambda^m(E_0)=E_0$. In such a case $\{z: z^m = 1 \} \subseteq H$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (ii) The family of minimal nonzero orthogonal projections $\{ E_k: k \in \mathbb{Z} \}$ where $E_k= \Lambda^k(E_0)$
for $k \ge 0$ and $E_k= S^*_IE_0S_I$ for $k < 0$ where $|I|=-k$ and independent of multi-index $I$ generates
the centre and $H=S^1$; 

\vskip 1em
\noindent (b) $\Lambda(E)=\tilde{\Lambda}(E) $ for any $E$ in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (c) If $\Lambda(E_0)=E_0$ then $E_0=1$.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
nodes.statement_short: The centre of pi(tilde UHF_d tensor UHF_d)'' is completely atomic, generated by Lambda-orbits of a minimal projection E_0, either periodic or indexed by Z.
assumptions: Let $\omega,\psi$ be as in Proposition 3.2
conclusions: Then the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is completely atomic

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement:
Let $E' \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)'$ be the projection onto the subspace generated
by the vectors $\{ S_IS^*_J\tilde{S}_{I'}S^*_{J'}\Omega,\; |I|=|J|,|I'|=|J'| < \infty \}$ and $\pi_{\Omega}$ be the restriction
of the representation $\pi$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ to the cyclic subspace ${\mathcal H}_{\Omega}$ generated by
$\Omega$. Identifying ${\mathcal B}$ with $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ we check that $\pi_{\omega}$ is unitary
equivalent to $\pi_{\Omega}$. Thus $\pi_{\Omega}$ is a factor representation. 

\vskip 1em
For any projection $E$ in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$, via the unitary equivalence, we note 
that $EE'=E'EE'$ is an element in the centre of $\pi_{\Omega}(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. $\omega$ being a 
factor state we conclude that $EE'$ is a scalar multiple of $E'$ and so we have
\begin{equation}
EE'=\omega(E)E'
\end{equation}
Thus we also have $EYE'=\omega(E)YE'$ for all $Y \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)'$ and so 
\begin{equation}
EE_0=\omega(E)E_0
\end{equation}
 
\vskip 1em
Since $EE'$ is a projection and $E' \ne 0$, we have $\omega(E)=\omega(E)^2$. Thus $\omega(E)=1$ or $0$. So, for such an element $E$,
the following is true:

\noindent (i) If $E \le E_0$ then either $E=0$ or $E=E_0$ i.e. $E_0$ is a minimal projection in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$

\noindent (ii) $\omega(E)=1$ if and only if $E \ge E_0$ 

\noindent (iii) $\omega(E)=0$ if and only if $EE_0=0$.

\vskip 1em
As $\Lambda(E_0)$ is a projection in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ by our last proposition i.e. Proposition 
3.2 (c), we have either $\omega(\Lambda(E_0))=1$ or $0$. Since $\Lambda(E_0) \neq 0$ by the injective property of the endomorphism, 
we have either $\Lambda(E_0) \ge E_0$ or $\Lambda(E_0)E_0=0$. In case $\Lambda(E_0) \ge E_0$ we have $S^*_iE_0S_i \le S^*_i\Lambda(E_0)S_i=E_0$ 
for all $1 \le i \le d$. If so, $S^*_iE_0S_i$ being a non-zero projection in the centre of $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ (Proposition 3.2 (c) ), 
by (i) we have $E_0=\Lambda(E_0)$. Thus we have either $\Lambda(E_0)=E_0$ or $\Lambda(E_0)E_0=0$. 

\vskip 1em
If $\Lambda(E_0)E_0=0$, we have $\Lambda(E_0) \le I-E_0$ and by Cuntz's relation we check that
$E_0 \le I - S^*_iE_0S_i$ and $S^*_jS^*_iE_0S_iS_j \le I- S^*_jE_0S_j$ for all $1 \le i,j \le d$.
So we also have $E_0S^*_jS^*_iE_0S_iS_jE_0 \le E_0- E_0S^*_jE_0S_jE_0=E_0$. Thus we have either
$E_0S^*_jS^*_iE_0S_iS_jE_0= 0$ or $E_0S^*_jS^*_iE_0S_iS_jE_0=E_0$ as $S^*_jS^*_iE_0S_iS_j$ is an element
in the centre by Proposition 3.2 (c). So either we have $\Lambda^2(E_0)E_0=0$ or $\Lambda^2(E_0) \le E_0$. 
$\Lambda$ being an injective map we either have $\Lambda^2(E_0)E_0=0$ or $\Lambda^2(E_0)= E_0.$

\vskip 1em
More generally we check that if $\Lambda(E_0)E_0=0, \Lambda^2(E_0)E_0=0,..\Lambda^k(E_0)E_0=0$ for some $k \ge 1$
then either $\Lambda^{k+1}(E_0)E_0=0$ or $\Lambda^{k+1}(E_0)=E_0$. To verify that first we check that in such a
case $E_0 \le I- S^*_IE_0S_I$ for all $|I|=n$ and then following the same steps as before to check that $S^*_iS^*_IE_0S_IS_i
\le I-S^*E_0S_i$ for all $i$. Thus we have $E_0S^*_iS^*_IE_0S_IS_iE_0 \le E_0$ and arguing as before we complete the proof
of the claim that either $\Lambda^{k+1}(E_0)E_0=0$ or $\Lambda^{k+1}(E_0)=E_0.$ 

\vskip 1em
We summarize now by saying that $E_0,\Lambda(E_0),..,\Lambda^{m-1}(E_0)$ are mutually orthogonal projections with $m \ge 1$ possibly 
be infinite, if not then $\Lambda^m(E_0)=E_0$. 

\vskip 1em
Let $\pi_k,\;k \ge 0$ be the representation $\pi$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ restricted to the
subspace $\Lambda^k(E_0)$. The representation $\pi_0$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ is 
isomorphic to the representation $\pi$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ restricted to $E'$ and thus
quasi-equivalent. For a general discussion on quasi-equivalence we refer to section 2.4.4 in [BR vol-1]. Since $\omega$ is a factor state, 
$\pi_0$ is a factor representation. We claim now that each $\pi_k$ is a factor representation. We fix any $k \ge 1$ and let $X$ be an element 
in the centre of $\pi_k(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)$. Then for any $|I|=k$, $S^*_IE_kS_I=E_0$ and so $S^*_IXS_I$ is an element 
in the centre of $\pi_0(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)$ by Proposition 3.2 (d). Further $S_I^*XS_I= S^*_IXS_IS^*_JS_J = S^*_JXS_J$ 
for all $|J|=|I|=k$. $\pi_0$ being a factor representation, we have $S^*_IXS_I= c E_0$ for some scalar $c$ independent of the multi-index we choose $|I|=k$. 
Hence $c \Lambda_k(E_0) = \sum _{|J|=k } S_JS^*_IXS_IS_J^*=\sum _{|J|=k } S_JS^*_IS_IS_J^*X= X$ as $X$ is an element in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)$. 
Thus for each $k \ge 1$, $\pi_k$ is a factor representation as $\pi_0$ is so.  

\vskip 1em
We also note that $\Lambda(E_0)\tilde{\Lambda}(E_0) \neq 0$. Otherwise we have $<S_i\Omega,\tilde{S}_j\Omega>=0$
for all $i,j$ and so $<\Omega,\tilde{S}_jS^*_i\Omega>=0$ for all $i,j$ as $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ commutes with 
$\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$. However $\tilde{S}^*_i\Omega=S^*_i\Omega$ and $\sum_i \tilde{S}_i\tilde{S}^*_i=1$ 
which leads a contradiction. Hence $\Lambda(E_0)\tilde{\Lambda}(E_0) \neq 0$. As $\pi$ restricted to 
$\Lambda(E_0)$ is a factor state and both $\Lambda(E_0)$ and $\tilde{\Lambda}(E_0)$ are elements in the 
centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF})''$, by Proposition 3.2 (d), 
we conclude that $\Lambda(E_0)=\tilde{\Lambda}(E_0).$ Using the commuting property of the endomorphisms $\Lambda$ 
and $\tilde{\Lambda}$, we verify by a simple induction method that $\Lambda^k(E_0) = \tilde{\Lambda}^k(E_0)$ 
for all $k \ge 1$. Thus the sequence of orthogonal projections $E_0, \tilde{\Lambda}(E_0),...$, are also periodic with same 
period or aperiodic according as the sequence of orthogonal projections $E_0,\Lambda(E_0),...$ is. 

\vskip 1em
If $\Lambda^m(E_0)=E_0$ for some $m \ge 1$ then we check that $\sum_{0 \le k \le m-1} \Lambda^k(E_0)$ is a 
$\Lambda$ and as well $\tilde{\Lambda}$-invariant projection and thus equal to $1$ by the cyclic property of 
$\Omega$ for $\pi({\mathcal O}_d \otimes \tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$. In such a case we set $V_z=\sum_{0 \le k \le m-1} z^kE_k$ for $z \in S^1$ 
for which $z^m=1$ and check that $\Lambda(V_z)= \sum_{0 \le k \le m-1}z^k\Lambda(E_k)=\sum_{0 \le k \le m-1} z^k E_{k+1}= \bar{z} V_z$ 
where $E_m=E_0$ and so by the Cuntz relations we have $V^*_zS_iV_z= \bar{z}S_i$ for all $1 \le i \le d$. Following the same 
steps we also have $\tilde{\Lambda}(V_z)=\bar{z}V_z$ and so $V^*_z\tilde{S}_iV^*_z=\bar{z}\tilde{S}_i$ for $ 1 \le i \le d$. 
Thus $V_z=U_z$ for all $z \in H_0 = \{z: z^m=1 \} \subseteq H$. 

\vskip 1em
Now we consider the case where $E_0,\Lambda(E_0),..\Lambda^k(E_0),..$ is a sequence of aperiodic orthogonal
projections. We extend the family of projections $\{E_k:\;k \in \mathbb{Z} \}$ to all integers by 
 
$$E_k=\Lambda^k(E_0)\;\; \mbox{for all}\;\; k \ge 1$$
and
$$E_k = S^*_IE_0S_I\;\; \mbox{for all}\;\;k \le 1,\;\;\mbox{where}\;\; |I|=-k$$
We claim that the definition of $\{ E_k;\;k \le -1 \}$ does depends only on length of the multi-index 
$I$ that we choose. We may choose any other $J$ so that $|J|=|I|$ and check the following identity: 
$$S^*_IE_0S_I = S^*_IE_0S_IS^*_JS_J=S^*_IS_IS^*_JE_0S_J=S^*_JE_0S_J$$ 
where $E_0$, being an element in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$, 
commutes with $S_IS_J^*$ as $|I|=|J|$. Further $\Lambda^k(E_0)=\tilde{\Lambda}^k(E_0)$ ensures that 
$S_I\tilde{S}_J^*$ commutes with $E_0$ for all $|I|=|J|=k$ and $k \ge 1$. Hence we also have 
$$E_{-k}=S^*_IE_0S_I\tilde{S}^*_J\tilde{S}_J=\tilde{S}^*_JE_0\tilde{S}_J$$ 
for all $|J|=|I|=k$ and $k \ge 1$. Now we claim that 
$$\Lambda(E_k) = \tilde{\Lambda}(E_k) = E_{k+1}$$ 
for all $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. For $k \ge 0$ we have nothing to prove. For $k \le -1$ we check that the following steps
$$\Lambda(S^*_IE_0S_I)$$
$$=\sum_j S_jS^*_iS^*_{I'}E_0S_{I'}S_iS_j^*$$
$$=\sum_jS^*_{I'}E_0S_{I'} S_jS^*_iS_iS_j^* = S^*_{I'}E_0S_{I'}$$
where we have $I=(I',i)$ and used the fact that elements $S_jS^*_i$ commutes with $\{ E_k: k \in \mathbb{Z} \}$, which are elements in the centre of 
$\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. For a proof that 
$\tilde{\Lambda}(E_k)=E_{k+1}$ we may follow the same steps as 
$E_k=\tilde{S}^*_IX\tilde{S}_I$ where $|I|=-k$ and $k \le -1$. 

\vskip 1em
We also claim that $\{ E_k: k \in \mathbb{Z} \}$ is an orthogonal family of non-zero projections. To that end we choose any two elements
say $E_k,E_m,\;k \ne m$ and use endomorphism $\Lambda^n$ for $n$ large enough so that both $n+k \ge 0 , n+m  \ge 0$
to conclude that $\Lambda^n(E_kE_m) = E_{k+n}E_{k+m}=0$ as $k+n \ne k+m$. $\Lambda$ being an injective map we get
the required orthogonal property. Thus $\sum_{ k \in \mathbb{Z}} E_k$ being an invariant projection for both $\Lambda$ and
$\tilde{\Lambda}$ we get by cyclic property of $\Omega$ that $\sum_{ k \in \mathbb{Z}} E_k=I$. Let $\pi_k,\; k \le -1$ be the representation $\pi$ 
of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ restricted to the subspace $E_k$. Going along the same line as above, we verify that for 
each $k \le -1$, $\pi_k$ is a factor representation of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$. We also set $V_z= \sum_{-\infty < k 
< \infty} z^k E_k$ for all $z \in S^1$ and check that $\Lambda(V_z)=\bar{z}V_z$ and also $\tilde{\Lambda}(V_z)=\bar{z}V_z$. Hence $S^1=H$ 
as $H$ is a closed subset of $S^1$. This completes the proof of (a). Proof of (b) and (c) are now simple consequence of the proof of (a).
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
nodes.statement_short: Factor property of omega makes central projections act as 0/1 on E', so E_0 is minimal; iterating Lambda gives a periodic or aperiodic orthogonal orbit of factor representations.

nodes.name: Algebra I_0
nodes.statement: It is clear that ${\mathcal I}$ contains ${\mathcal I}_0:=^{\mbox{def}} \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)'' \vee \{U_z: z \in H \}''$.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:

nodes.name: Representations pi'_k on F_k
nodes.statement: For each $k \in \hat{H}$, let $\pi'_k$ be the representation $\pi$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ restricted to $F_k$.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:

nodes.name: Each pi'_k is pure if pi'_0 is pure
nodes.statement:
We claim that each $\pi'_k$ 
is pure if $\pi'_0$ is pure.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
assumptions: $\pi'_0$ is pure

nodes.name: Proof that each pi'_k is pure
nodes.statement:
Fix any $k \in \hat{H}$ and let $X$ be an element in the commutant of $\pi'_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ then 
$S^*_IF_kS_I = S^*_I\Lambda^k(F_0)S_I = F_0$ as $S^*_JS_I$ commutes with $F_0$ for $|I|=|J|=k$ and further for any $|I|=|J|$, $S_I^*XS_IS_J^*S_J=S_I^*S_IS_J^*XS_J=S^*_JXS_J$ 
as $X$ commutes with $S_IS_J^*$ with $|I|=|J|$. Thus by Proposition 3.2 (c) $S^*_IXS_I$ is an element in commutant of $\pi'_0(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ 
for any $|I|=k$ and thus $S_I^*XS_I= c F_0$ for some scalar $c$ independent of $|I|=k$ as $\pi'_0$ is pure. We use 
the commuting property of $X$ with $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ to conclude that 
$X = c \Lambda^k(E_0)$ for some scalar $c$. If $k \le -1$ we employ the same method but with the endomorphism 
$\Lambda^{-k}$ so that $\Lambda^{-k}(X)$ is an element in the commutant of 
$\pi'_0(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. Thus $\sum_{I:|I|=-k }S_IXS^*_I = c I$ and by 
the injective property of the endomorphism we get $X$ is a scalar. Thus we conclude that each $\pi'_k$ is 
pure if $\pi'_0$ is pure.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
nodes.statement_short: Pull back commutant elements by X -> S_I^* X S_I to the commutant of pi'_0, where purity forces scalars; injectivity of Lambda handles negative k.

nodes.name: pi_k is quasi-equivalent to pi'_k
nodes.statement:
Next we claim that for each fixed $k \in \hat{H_0}$, the representation $\pi_k$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ defined in the proof of Proposition 3.3 is quasi-equivalent to representation $\pi'_k$ ( here we recall 
$\hat{H_0} \subseteq \hat{H}$ as $H_0 \subseteq H$ ).
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:

nodes.name: Proof that pi_k is quasi-equivalent to pi'_k
nodes.statement:
That $\pi'_0$ is quasi-equivalent to 
$\pi_0$ follows as they are isomorphic by construction. In the proof of Proposition 3.3 we defined representation $\pi_k$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)'$ for all $k \in \hat{H}_0$ associated with minimal projections 
$\{E_k: k \in \hat{H}_0 \}$. More generally for any $k \in \hat{H}$, we denote $\pi_k$ for the restriction of $\pi$ to the minimal central projections 
$E_k$ on the subspace span by $\{\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)'f: \forall \;\; f\;\; \in {\mathcal H} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} \tilde{{\mathcal H}}, \;\;F_kf=f \}$. 
So each $E_k$ is a minimal central element containing $F_k$. However two such elements i.e. 
$E_k$ and $E_j$ are either equal or mutually orthogonal being minimal. Thus $\{E_k: k \in \hat{H} \} = \{E_k: k \in \hat{H}_0 \}$
and quasi-equivalence follows as $\pi_k$ is isomorphic with $\pi'_k$ for all $k \in \hat{H}_0$.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
nodes.statement_short: Each minimal central projection E_k contains F_k, and minimal central projections are equal or orthogonal, so the restrictions agree up to isomorphism.

nodes.name: Projection F'_0
nodes.statement:
We now set 
$$F'_0=[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega]$$
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:

nodes.name: F'_0 <= F_0
nodes.statement: For a vector $f$ if $F'_0f=f$ then $U_zf=f$ for all $z \in H$ and thus $F'_0 \le F_0$.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:

nodes.name: F'_0 = F_0 when omega is pure
nodes.statement: We prove in following text that equality holds if $\omega$ is pure.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
assumptions: $\omega$ is pure

nodes.name: Proof that F'_0 = F_0 for pure omega
nodes.statement:
First we consider the case when $H=\{z: z^n=1\}$. Projections $\Lambda(F'_0)$ and $\tilde{\Lambda}(F'_0)$ are elements in $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)'$ by Proposition 3.3. The representation $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ restricted to both the projections $\Lambda(F'_0),\tilde{\Lambda}(F'_0)$ are pure as well. A pull back by the map $X \rightarrow S^*_iXS_i$ with any $1 \le i \le d$ will do the job for the projection $\Lambda(F'_0)$. Thus 
$\Lambda(F'_0)\tilde{\Lambda}(F'_0)\Lambda(F'_0) = c \Lambda(F'_0)$ for 
some scalar. By pulling back with the action $X \rightarrow S^*_i X S_i$ we get
$F'_0 S^*_i\tilde{\Lambda}(F'_0)S_i F'_0 = cF'_0$ and so 
$$c=<\Omega,S^*_i\tilde{\Lambda}(F'_0)S_i\Omega>$$
$$=\sum_k <\Omega,S_k S^*_iF'_0S_iS^*_k\Omega>$$
as $\tilde{S}^*_k\Omega=S^*_k\Omega$ and further $F'_0$ commutes 
with $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)$ and thus 
$$c=\sum_k <\Omega, S_k S_k^*\Omega>=1$$
This shows that $\tilde{\Lambda}(F'_0) \ge \Lambda(F'_0)$. Interchanging the role
of $\Lambda$ and $\tilde{\Lambda}$ we conclude that $\Lambda(F'_0)=\tilde{\Lambda}(F'_0)$. Now it essentially follows along the same line  
$\Lambda^k(F'_0)=\tilde{\Lambda}^k(F'_0)$ for all $k \ge 1$. 
By Proposition 2.5 we also note that 
$$\Lambda^n(F'_0)=F'_0=\tilde{\Lambda}^n(F_0)$$ 
as $H=\{z : z^n =1 \}$. Thus $F'=\sum_{0 \le k \le n-1}\Lambda(F'_0)$ is a $\Lambda$ and as well $\tilde{\Lambda}$ invariant projection. Since 
$F'\Omega=\Omega$ we conclude by the cyclic property of $\Omega$ for $\pi({\mathcal O}_d \otimes \tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ that $F'=1$. Since $\Lambda^k(F'_0) 
\le F_k$ and $\sum_k F_k=1 $, we conclude that $\Lambda^k(F_0)=F_k$. In such a case we may check that  
$$F_k = [\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''S^*_I\Omega: |I|=n-k]$$ 
for $1 \le k \le n-1$. 

\vskip 1em
Similarly in case $H=S^1$ and $\omega$ is pure we also have $F_0=F'_0$ and 
for $k \ge 1$ 
$$F_k=[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''S_I\Omega: |I|= k]$$
$$F_{-k}=[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''S^*_I\Omega: |I|=k]$$
Thus we have got an explicit description of the complete atomic centre of ${\mathcal I}$ 
when $\omega$ is a pure state.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on H finite or the circle: purity gives Lambda(F'_0)=tilde Lambda(F'_0), and summing the orbit yields an invariant projection equal to 1 by cyclicity.

nodes.name: Proposition 3.4 (gauge-invariant elements and purity)
nodes.statement:
Let $\omega,\psi$ and Popescu system $({\mathcal K},{\mathcal M},v_k,\Omega)$ be as in Proposition 3.3. Then 

\noindent (a) $\{\beta_z: z \in H \}$ invariant elements in $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d)''$ ( as well as in 
$\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ ) are equal to $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. 

\noindent (b) ${\mathcal I}={\mathcal I}_0$ if and only if $\omega$ is pure. 

Further the following statements are equivalent: 

\noindent (c) ${\mathcal I} = \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$; 

\noindent (d) $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d)''= {\mathcal B}(\tilde{{\mathcal H}} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} {\mathcal H})$;

\noindent (e) $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d )''= {\mathcal B}(\tilde{{\mathcal H}} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} {\mathcal H})$;

\vskip 1em
In such a case (i.e. if any of (c),(d) and (e) is true ) the following statements are also true: 

\noindent (f) $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is a type-I von-Neumann algebra with centre equal 
to $\{ U_z: z \in H \}''$ where $U_z$ is defined in Proposition 3.2. 

\noindent (g) $\omega$ is a pure state on ${\mathcal B}$. 

\vskip 1em
Conversely if $\omega$ is a pure state then $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is a type-I von-Neumann 
algebra with centre equal to $\{U_z: z \in H_0 \}''$ where $H_0$ is a subgroup of $H$.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
nodes.statement_short: The H-invariant part of the amalgamated algebra is the UHF part; I = I_0 iff omega is pure, and the equivalent conditions (c)-(e) imply type-I structure and purity.
assumptions: Let $\omega,\psi$ and Popescu system $({\mathcal K},{\mathcal M},v_k,\Omega)$ be as in Proposition 3.3.
conclusions: (b) ${\mathcal I}={\mathcal I}_0$ if and only if $\omega$ is pure.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.4
nodes.statement:
Along the same line of the proof of Proposition 2.5 (b) we get $\{\beta_z: z \in H \}$ invariant elements 
in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ is $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ where factor property 
of $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ is crucial as in proof of Proposition 2.5 (b). Same holds for $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ as 
$\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ is a factor. Here we comment that factor property of $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ can be
ensured whenever $\psi$ is an extremal element in $K_{\omega'}$ (See Proposition 3.2 (a) ). 

\vskip 1em
For (b) we will first prove ${\mathcal I}_0={\mathcal I}$ if $\omega$ is pure. As by definition ${\mathcal I}_0 \subseteq {\mathcal I}$, it is enough if we show 
${\mathcal I}'_0 \subseteq {\mathcal I}'$. Let $X \in {\mathcal I}'_0$ i.e. $X$ commutes with $\{ U_z:z \in H\}''$ and $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes 
\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. For each $k \in \hat{H}$, $F_kXF_k$ is an element in the commutant of $F_k\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes 
\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''F_k$. $\omega$ being pure each representation $\pi$ restricted to $F_k$ is irreducible and thus
$F_kXF_k = c_k F_k$ for some scalars $c_k$. Hence $X=\sum_k c_k F_k \in {\mathcal I}'=\{U_z: z \in H \}''$. 

\vskip 1em
For the converse we need to show that the restriction of $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes 
\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ to $F'_0$ is pure. Let $X$ be an element on the subspace $F'_0$ and in the commutant 
of $F'_0\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''F'_0$, ( which in our earlier notation $E'$ in Proposition 3.3 ). 
Then $X$ commutes with each $F_k$ for $k \in \hat{H}$ and $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes 
\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''F_k$ as $F'_0 \le F_0$ and $F_k$ are orthogonal to 
$F'_0$ for $k \neq 0$. So $X$ commutes with $\{U_z: z \in H \}''$ and 
$\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ i.e. $X \in {\mathcal I}'_0$. By our assumption ${\mathcal I}_0={\mathcal I}$, we have now
$X \in {\mathcal I}'$ which is equal to $\{F_k: k \in \hat{H} \}''$ and so $X=cF_0$ 
for some scalar $c_0$. This shows that $F'_0=F_0$ and $\omega$ is pure.    

\vskip 1em
(c) implies (d): $\{U_z: z \in H \}$ is a commuting family of unitaries such that $\beta_z(X)=U_zXU_z^*$ and 
thus by (c) $\{U_z: z \in H \}'' \subseteq \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. Let $X$ be an 
element in the commutant of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d)''$. Then 
$X$ commutes also with $\{U_z: z \in H \}''$ and thus $X \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ by (c).
Hence $X$ is an element in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ and so 
$X=\sum_k c_kE_k$ where $E_k$ are the minimal projections in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ 
given in Proposition 3.3. However $X$ also 
commutes with $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ by our assumption (c) and $\Lambda(E_k)=E_{k+1}$ for $k \in \hat{H}$.  
So $c_k=c_{k+1}$ and $X$ is a scalar multiple of unit operator. Hence (d) follows from (c). Along the same line we prove 
(c) implies (e). For a proof for (d) implies (c) and (e) implies (c), we simply apply (a).   

\vskip 1em
Now we will prove (f) and (g). That $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is 
a type-I von-Neumann algebra ( with completely atomic centre ) follows by a theorem of [So] once we use (c). In the proof 
of Proposition 3.3 we have proved that the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is 
$\{U_z: z \in H_0 \}''$ where $H_0 \subseteq H$. For equality in the present situation we simply use (c), as $\beta_w(U_z)=U_z$
for all $w,z \in H$, to conclude that $U_z$ is in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. 

\vskip 1em
If (c) holds then ${\mathcal I}_0={\mathcal I}$ and thus (g) follows by (b). Here we will give another proof using the same idea to prove (f). 
Let $X$ be an element in the commutant of $\pi_0(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$, where $\pi_0$ is the factor 
representation on the minimal central projection $E_0$ defined in Proposition 3.3. Then $X$ commutes with 
$\{U_z: z \in H \}''$ and so by (c) $X$ in an element in $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. 
So $X$ is in the centre of $\pi_0(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. $\pi_0$ being a factor representation
$X$ is a scalar multiple of $E_0$. Thus $\pi_0$ is an irreducible representation and so $\omega$ is pure. 

\vskip 1em
By Proposition 3.1 we recall that $\pi'_0$ is unitary equivalent to the GNS representation of $({\mathcal B},\omega)$. 
Thus $\pi'_0$ is irreducible if and only if $\omega$ is pure. So for a pure state $\omega$, 
for each $k \in \hat{H}_0$, $\pi_k$ being quasi-equivalent to $\pi'_k$, $\pi_k$ is a type-I factor 
representation of $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. This completes the proof.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
nodes.statement_short: Irreducibility of the restrictions to F_k under purity identifies I'_0 with the algebra of U_z; Stormer's theorem gives type-I structure.

nodes.name: Proposition 3.5 (support projections in the amalgamated representation)
nodes.statement:
Let $\omega$ be an extremal translation invariant state on ${\mathcal B}$ and $\psi$ be an extremal 
element $\psi$ in $K_{\omega}$. We consider the Popescu elements $({\mathcal K},v_k:1 \le k \le d, {\mathcal M},\Omega)$
as in Proposition 2.4 for the dual Popescu elements and associated amalgamated representation $\pi$ of
${\mathcal O}_d \otimes \tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d$ as described in Proposition 3.1. Let ${\mathcal E}$ and $\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ be the support 
projections of the state $\psi$ in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ and $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ respectively. Let ${\mathcal F}$ and $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ be the projections 
$[\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''\Omega]$ and $[\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)\Omega]$ respectively. Then the following holds:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (a) $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d)''= {\mathcal B}( \tilde{{\mathcal H}} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} {\mathcal H})$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (b) $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''=\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'$ if and only if $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''{\mathcal E}=\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'{\mathcal E}$; 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (c) $Q={\mathcal E} \tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ is the support projection of the state $\psi$ in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$
and also in $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''{\mathcal E}$. Further $P={\mathcal E} {\mathcal F} \le Q$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (d) If ${\mathcal E} {\mathcal F} = \tilde{{\mathcal E}}\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ then ${\mathcal E}=\tilde{{\mathcal F}},\;\tilde{{\mathcal E}}={\mathcal F},\;P=Q$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (e) If $P=Q$ then the following statements are true:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (i) ${\mathcal M}'= \tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ where $\tilde{{\mathcal M}} = \{ P\tilde{S}_iP: 1 \le i \le d
\}''$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (ii) $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)' = \pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (f) If $P=[\tilde{{\mathcal M}}\Omega]$ then ${\mathcal M}'=\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$; 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (g) $\omega$ is pure on ${\mathcal B}$ if and only if there exists a sequence of elements $x_n \in {\mathcal M}$ such that for each $m \ge 0$ 
$x_{n+m}\tau_n(x) \rightarrow \phi(x)1$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ in strong operator topology, equivalently $\phi(\tau_n(x)x_{n+m}^*x_{n+m}\tau_n(y)) \rightarrow \phi(x)\phi(y)$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for 
all $x,y \in {\mathcal M}$ where ${\mathcal M} = \{ v_i=PS_iP: 1 \le i \le d \}''$ and $\tau(x)=\sum_{1 \le k \le d}v_kxv_k^*,\;\;x \in {\mathcal M}$; Same holds true if we replace ${\mathcal M}_0$ for 
${\mathcal M}$ where ${\mathcal M}_0=\{x \in {\mathcal M}: \beta_z(x)=x; z \in H \}$.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
nodes.statement_short: Relates support projections E, tilde E and cyclic projections F, tilde F; P=Q forces M'=tilde M and pi(O_d)'=pi(tilde O_d)''; purity is characterised by an asymptotic condition on tau.
assumptions: Let $\omega$ be an extremal translation invariant state on ${\mathcal B}$ and $\psi$ be an extremal element $\psi$ in $K_{\omega}$.
conclusions: (e) If $P=Q$ then the following statements are true:

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.5
nodes.statement:
(a) is a restatement of Proposition 3.2 (a). ${\mathcal E}$ ( $\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ ) being the support projection of
the state $\psi$ in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ ( $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ ) and $\psi = \psi \Lambda$ we have $\Lambda({\mathcal E}) \ge {\mathcal E}$ 
and further we have ${\mathcal E}=[\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'\Omega] \ge [\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''\Omega]$ and hence increasing projections in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$, 
$\Lambda^n({\mathcal E}) \uparrow I$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ because $\Omega$ is cyclic for $\pi({\mathcal O}_d \otimes \tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ in ${\mathcal H} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} \tilde{{\mathcal H}}$ 
and limiting projection being in the commutant of $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ as well i.e. since $\Lambda(Y)=Y$ implies $Y \in \pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ by Cuntz relations.   

\vskip 1em 
We set von-Neumann algebras ${\mathcal N}_1=\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'{\mathcal E}$ and ${\mathcal N}_2=\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''{\mathcal E}$. By our construction we have $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)'' 
\subseteq \pi({\mathcal O}_d)' $ and so ${\mathcal N}_2 \subseteq {\mathcal N}_1$. Since $\Lambda^n({\mathcal E}) \uparrow I$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ in strong operator topology, 
two operators in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'$ are same if their actions are same on ${\mathcal E}$. So (b) is true. 

\vskip 1em 
For (c) we note that $Q={\mathcal E}\tilde{{\mathcal E}} \in {\mathcal N}_2 \subseteq {\mathcal N}_1$ and claim that $Q$ is the support projection of the state $\psi$ in ${\mathcal N}_2$. 
To that end let $x{\mathcal E} \ge 0$ for some $x \in \pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ so that $\psi(QxQ)=0$. As $\Lambda^k(x{\mathcal E}) \ge 0$ for all $k \ge 1$ and $\Lambda^k({\mathcal E}) \rightarrow I$ 
we conclude that $x \ge 0$. As ${\mathcal E} \Omega=\Omega$ and thus $\psi(\tilde{{\mathcal E}}x\tilde{{\mathcal E}})=\psi(QxQ)=0$, we conclude
$\tilde{{\mathcal E}}x\tilde{{\mathcal E}}=0$, $\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ being the support projection for $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$. Hence $QxQ=0$.
As $\psi(Q)=1$, we complete the proof of the claim that $Q$ is the support of $\psi$ in ${\mathcal N}_2$. Similarly $Q$ is also
the support projection of the state $\psi$ in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$. This completes the proof of (c).

\vskip 1em 
Thus if ${\mathcal E} {\mathcal F}=\tilde{{\mathcal E}}\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$, we get $\Lambda^n({\mathcal E}){\mathcal F}=\tilde{{\mathcal E}} \Lambda^n(\tilde{{\mathcal F}})$ and 
${\mathcal E} \tilde{\Lambda}({\mathcal F}) = \tilde{\Lambda}(\tilde{{\mathcal E}})\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ and thus taking limit we get 
${\mathcal F}=\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ and ${\mathcal E}=\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. It is obvious now that $P={\mathcal E} {\mathcal F} = {\mathcal E} \tilde{{\mathcal E}}=Q$. This completes 
the proof of (d). 

\vskip 1em
As ${\mathcal E} \in \pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ and $\tilde{{\mathcal E}} \in \pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ we check that von-Neumann algebras 
${\mathcal M}^1 = Q \pi({\mathcal O}_d)'' Q$ and $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}^1 = Q \pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d) Q$ acting on $Q$ satisfy 
$\tilde{{\mathcal M}}^1 \subseteq {\mathcal M}^{1'}$. Now we explore that $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d)''= 
{\mathcal B}({\mathcal H} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} \tilde{{\mathcal H}})$ and note that in such a case $Q\pi( \tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d )''Q$ 
is the set of all bounded operators on the Hilbert subspace $Q$. As ${\mathcal E} \in \pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ and 
$\tilde{{\mathcal E}} \in \pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ we check that together ${\mathcal M}^1 = Q \pi({\mathcal O}_d)'' Q$ and 
$\tilde{{\mathcal M}}^1 = Q \pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d) Q$ generate all bounded operators on $Q$. Thus both ${\mathcal M}^1$ 
and $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}^1$ are factors. The canonical states $\psi$ on ${\mathcal M}^1$ and $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}^1$ are 
faithful and normal. We set $l_k=QS_kQ$ and $\tilde{l}_k=Q\tilde{S}_kQ,\; 1 \le k \le d$ and recall 
that $v_k=PS_kP$ and $\tilde{v}_k=P\tilde{S}_kP,\; 1 \le k \le d$. We note that $Pl_kP=v_k$ and 
$P\tilde{l}_kP = \tilde{v}_k$ where we recall that, by our construction, $P$ is the support projection of 
the state $\psi$ in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''_{|}[\pi({\mathcal O}_d)\Omega]$. $Q$ being the support projection of 
$\pi({\mathcal O}_d)\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$, by Theorem 2.4 applied to Cuntz elements $\{S_i\tilde{E}: 1 \le i \le d \}$, 
$\tilde{{\mathcal E}} \pi({\mathcal O}_d)'\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ is order isomorphic to ${\mathcal M}^{1'}$ via the map $X \rightarrow QXQ$. As the projection 
${\mathcal F}=[\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''\Omega] \in \pi({\mathcal O}_d)'$, we check that the element $Q{\mathcal F}\tilde{{\mathcal E}}Q \in {\mathcal M}^{1'}$. However 
$Q{\mathcal F} \tilde{{\mathcal E}}Q={\mathcal E}\tilde{{\mathcal E}}{\mathcal F}\tilde{{\mathcal E}}{\mathcal E}=QPQ=P$ and thus $P \in {\mathcal M}^{1'}$. We also check that 
${\mathcal M}^1\Omega={\mathcal M}^1P\Omega=P{\mathcal M}^1\Omega={\mathcal M} \Omega$ and thus $P=[{\mathcal M}^1\Omega]$. We set 
$\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ for the von-Neumann algebra generated by $\{\tilde{v}_k:\; 1 \le k \le d \}$. 

\vskip 1em 
So far our analysis did not use the hypothesis on statement (e) i.e. $P=Q$. For $P=Q$, we have 
${\mathcal M}^1={\mathcal M}$ and $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}^1=\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$. By order isomorphic property 
we get (i) is equivalent to $\tilde{{\mathcal E}} \pi({\mathcal O}_d)' \tilde{{\mathcal E}} = \tilde{{\mathcal E}} \pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ 
and taking commutant again we get $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''\tilde{{\mathcal E}} = \pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)'\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$. Now we invoke the first 
part of the argument changing the role or using the endomorphism $\tilde{\Lambda}$ we conclude that 
$\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''=\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)'$. This completes the proof of (e) provided we find a independent proof for (i) 
which is not so evident and this crucial point was not noticed in the proof given for Lemma 7.8 in [BJKW].  

\vskip 1em 
Now we will analyze the representation $\pi$ of $\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d$ which is pure to prove (i). To that end we note 
since $P=Q$ by our assumption, $\Omega$ is a common cyclic and separating vector for $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ and ${\mathcal M}'$.   
Thus we can get an endomorphism $\alpha: {\mathcal M}' \rightarrow \tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ defined by 
$$\alpha(y)=\tilde{{\mathcal J}}{\mathcal J} y {\mathcal J} \tilde{{\mathcal J}}$$ 
where $\tilde{{\mathcal J}}$ is the Tomita's conjugate operator associated with the cyclic and separating vector $\Omega$ for $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$  
( i.e. for $y \in {\mathcal M}'$, we have ${\mathcal J} y {\mathcal J} \in {\mathcal M} \subseteq \tilde{{\mathcal M}}'$ since $\tilde{{\mathcal M}} \subseteq {\mathcal M}'$. 
Since $\tilde{{\mathcal J}}\tilde{{\mathcal M}}'\tilde{{\mathcal J}}=\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$, we have $\alpha(y) \in \tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ ). We note that the general theory 
does not guarantee [AcC] that the endomorphism be Takesaki's canonical conditional expectation associated with $\phi$. If so then the modular 
automorphism group $(\sigma_t)$ of ${\mathcal M}'$ also preserves $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$. Thus $\sigma_z(x) \in \tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ for $-1 \le Im(z) \le 1$ 
if $x$ is an analytic element in $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$. Thus we would have got ${\mathcal J} v_k(\delta) {\mathcal J} = 
\sigma_{i \over 2}(\tilde{v}_k(\delta)) \in \tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ where $x(\delta)$ is average of 
$\sigma_t(x)$ with respect to Gaussian measure with variance $\delta > 0$. That $\tilde{v}_k(\delta)$ 
is an analytic element follows from the general Tomita-Takesaki theory [BR1]. Since $v_k(\delta) \rightarrow v_k$ in strong 
operator topology as $\delta \rightarrow 0$ and ${\mathcal M} = \{v_k: 1 \le k \le d \}''$ together with 
${\mathcal J} {\mathcal M} {\mathcal J} = {\mathcal M}'$ we arrived at $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}={\mathcal M}'$. In the following we avoid this tempting 
route and aim to explore the general representation theory of $C^*$-algebras [BR1,chapter 2].   

\vskip 1em 
We claim that ${\mathcal M}'=\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$. Suppose not i.e. $\tilde{{\mathcal M}} \subset {\mathcal M}'$. Then $\alpha(\tilde{{\mathcal M}})$ is a proper von-Neumann subalgebras 
of $\alpha({\mathcal M}') \subseteq \tilde{{\mathcal M}} $ being an into map and hence $\alpha(\tilde{{\mathcal M}})$ is a proper von-Neumann 
sub-algebra of $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$. Now consider the Popescu elements $({\mathcal K},\alpha(\tilde{v}_i),\Omega)$ and its dilation 
as in Theorem 2.1. Then by the commutant lifting theorem applied to pairs 
$(\tilde{v}_i),\alpha(\tilde{v}_i)$ we find a unitary operator $U$ on $\tilde{{\mathcal H}}$ so that 
$U\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''U^*$ is strictly contained in $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ ( Without loss of generality we can 
take the dilated Hilbert space for $({\mathcal K},\alpha(\tilde{v}_i),\Omega)$ to be same as $\tilde{{\mathcal H}}$ as there exists an 
isomorphism preserving ${\mathcal K}$, see the remark that follows after Theorem 2.1 ). We extend $U$ to a unitary operator 
on $\tilde{{\mathcal H}} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} {\mathcal H}$ and denote $\pi_u(x)=U \pi(x) U^*$ for $x \in \tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d$ which 
is unitary equivalent to the pure representation $\pi$ and $\pi_u(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ is strictly contained in 
$\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$. Now $\pi_u$ is also an amalgamated representation over the subspace ${\mathcal K}$ with 
$P_u=Q_u$. Thus we can repeat now same procedure with $\pi_u$ and so on. Note that the process won't terminate in finite 
time. Our aim is to find a contradiction from this using formal set theory.  

\vskip 1em 
To that end we use temporary notation $\pi_0$ for $\pi$ defined in last paragraph and $\pi$ will be used for a generic representation. 
Let ${\mathcal P}$ be the collection of representation $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega)$ quasi-equivalent to $\pi_0:\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d  
\rightarrow {\mathcal B}(\tilde{{\mathcal H}} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} {\mathcal H} )$ with a shift invariant vector state $\omega(x)=<\Omega,\pi(x)\Omega>$ i.e. 
$\omega(\pi(\theta(x))=\omega(\pi(x))$. So there exists cardinal numbers $n_{\pi},n_0(\pi)$ so that $n_{\pi}H_{\pi}$ is unitary 
equivalent to $n_0(\pi)\pi_0$. Thus given an element $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega)$ we can associate two cardinal numbers $n_{\pi}$ and $n_0(\pi)$ 
and without loss of generality we assume that $H_{\pi} \subseteq n_0(\pi)H_0$ and $n_{\pi}H_{\pi}=n_0(\pi)H_0.$  $\pi_0$ being a pure representation, 
any element $\pi \in {\mathcal P}$ is a type-I factor representation of $\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d $. The interesting point here that $\displaystyle{\oplus_{\pi \in {\mathcal P} }}\pi$ 
is also an element in ${\mathcal P}$ with associated cardinal numbers $\sum_{\pi} n_{\pi}$ and $\sum_{\pi} n_0(\pi)$. We say $(\pi_1,H_{\pi_1},\Omega^1) \prec (\pi_2,H_{\pi_2},\Omega^2)$ 
if there exists an isometry $U:n_{\pi_1} H_{\pi_1} \rightarrow n_{\pi_2} H_{\pi_2}$ so that 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (C1) For each $1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} $ we have 
$U \Omega^1_{\alpha} = \Omega^2_{\alpha'}$ for some 
$1 \le \alpha' \le n_{\pi_2}$;

\noindent (C2) $n_{\pi_2}\pi_2(x)E'_2 = U n_{\pi_1}\pi_1(x) U^* $ where ${\mathcal E}'_2 \in n_{\pi_2}\pi_2(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)'$; 
 
\noindent (C3) $U\oplus_{1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} }\pi^{\alpha}_1(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''U^* \subset \oplus_{1 \le 
\alpha \le n_{\pi_2}}\pi^{\alpha}_1(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''E'_2$. 

\vskip 1em 
That the partial order is non-reflexive follows as $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega) \prec (\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega)$ contradicts (C3) as $I=E_2'$. By our starting assumption that ${\mathcal M}' \neq \tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ 
we check that $\pi_0 \prec \pi_u$. Thus going via the isomorphism we also check that for a given element $\pi \in {\mathcal P}$ there exists an element $\pi' \in {\mathcal P}$ so that $\pi \prec \pi'$. 
Thus ${\mathcal P}_0$ is a non empty set and has at least one infinite chain. Partial order property follows easily. If $\pi_1 \prec \pi_2$ and $\pi_2 \prec \pi_3$ then $\pi_1 \prec \pi_3$. 
If $U_{12}$ and $U_{23}$ are isometric operators that satisfies (C1)-(C3) respectively, then $U_{13}=U_{23}U_{12}$ will do the job for $\pi_1$ and $\pi_3$. 
 
\vskip 1em 
However by Hausdorff maximality theorem there exists a non-empty maximal totally ordered subset ${\mathcal P}_0$ of ${\mathcal P}$. We claim that 
$\pi_{max}=\oplus_{\pi \in {\mathcal P}_0} \pi$ on $H_{\pi_{max}}=\oplus_{\pi \in {\mathcal P}_0} H_{\pi} $ is an upper bound 
in ${\mathcal P}_0$. That $\pi_{max} \in {\mathcal P}$ is obvious. Further given an element $(H_1,\pi_1,\Omega_1) \in {\mathcal P}_0$ there exists 
an element $(H_2,\pi_2,\Omega_2) \in {\mathcal P}_0$ so that $\pi_1 \prec \pi_2$ by our starting remark as $\pi_0 \prec \pi_u$. 
By extending isometry $U_{12}$ to an isometry from $H_1 \rightarrow n_{\pi_{max}} H_{\pi_{max}}$ trivially we get the 
required isometry that satisfies (C1),(C2) and (C3) where cardinal numbers $n_{\pi_{max}} = \sum_{\pi \in {\mathcal P}_0} 
n_{\pi} \in \aleph_0$. Thus by maximal property of ${\mathcal P}_0$ we have $\pi_{max} \in {\mathcal P}_0$. This brings a contradiction 
as by our construction $(\pi_{max},H_{\pi_{max}},\Omega) \prec (\pi_{max},H_{\pi_{max}},\Omega)$ 
as $\pi_{max} \in {\mathcal P}_0$ but partial order is strict. This contradicts our starting hypothesis that $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ is 
a proper subset of ${\mathcal M}'$. This completes the proof for (i) of (e) ${\mathcal M}'=\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ when $P=Q$.  

\vskip 1em 
In the proof of ${\mathcal M}'=\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ in (e), we have used equality $P=Q$ just to ensure that $\Omega$ is also a cyclic for $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ and $P=Q$ is used 
to prove $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)' = \pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$. So (f) follows by the proof of (e). 

\vskip 1em 
A proof for (g) is given in [Mo3] with ${\mathcal M}_0$. Here we will also give an alternative proof relating the criteria obtained in Proposition 3.4. 
To that end we claim that $$\bigcap_{n \ge 1}\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)')=\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'
\bigcap \pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)'.$$ That $\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)') \subseteq \{ \tilde{S}_I\tilde{S}^*_J: |I|=|J| < \infty \}'$ follows by 
Cuntz relation and thus $\bigcap_{n \ge 1}\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)') \subseteq \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'\bigcap 
\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)'$. For the reverse inclusion let $X \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'\bigcap \pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)'$. For $n \ge 1$, 
we choose $|I|=n$ and set $Y_n=\tilde{S}^*_IX\tilde{S}_I$. 
We check that it is independent of the index that we have chosen as 
$Y_n=\tilde{S}^*_IX\tilde{S}_I\tilde{S}^*_J\tilde{S}_J=\tilde{S}^*_I\tilde{S}_I\tilde{S}^*_JX \tilde{S}_J=\tilde{S}^*_JX\tilde{S}_J$ 
where in second equality we have used $X \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'$ and also 
$\Lambda^n(Y_n)=\sum_{|J|=n } \tilde{S}_J\tilde{S}^*_IX\tilde{S}_I\tilde{S}^*_J=X$. This proves the equality in the claim. Going along the same line we also get 
$$\bigcap_{n \ge 1}\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi({\mathcal O}_d)') = \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'\bigcap \pi({\mathcal O}_d)'= \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d)'.$$ 

\vskip 1em 
By Proposition 3.4 $\omega$ is pure if and only if the set above is trivial. Thus once more by Proposition 1.1 in [Ar2] and 
Theorem 2.4 in [Mo2], purity is equivalent to asymptotic relation $||\psi \tilde{\tau}^n -\phi|| \rightarrow 0$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ 
for any normal state $\psi$ on ${\mathcal M}'$ ( Here we recall by Proposition 2.4 
$P\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'P={\mathcal M}'$ as $P$ is also the support projection 
in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''{\mathcal F}$ and support projection of $\phi_{\Omega}$ in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'$ 
is ${\mathcal F}=[\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''\Omega]$, where commutant is taken in ${\mathcal B}({\mathcal K})$ ). 
By a duality argument Theorem 2.4 in [Mo3] we conclude that $\omega$ is pure if and only if there exists 
a sequence of elements $x_n \in {\mathcal M}$ so that for each $m \ge 0$, $x_{m+n}\tau_n(x) \rightarrow \phi(x)1$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for all $x \in {\mathcal M} \subseteq {\mathcal B}({\mathcal K})$. 
This completes the proof of (d) with ${\mathcal M}$. For the proof with ${\mathcal M}_0$ we need to show if part as only if part follows ${\mathcal M}_0$ being a subset of ${\mathcal M}$ and $\tau$ 
takes elements of ${\mathcal M}_0$ to itself. For if part we refer to Theorem 3.2 in [Mo3].
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
nodes.statement_short: Support-projection bookkeeping for (a)-(d); for (e) assume tilde M is proper in M', build a strictly increasing chain of quasi-equivalent representations and contradict Hausdorff maximality. (g) via Arveson and Mohari's duality.

nodes.name: Gauge-invariant part (M')_0
nodes.statement:
We set 
$$({\mathcal M}')_0 = \{x \in {\mathcal M}' : \beta_z(x)=x,\;\; z \in H \}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:

nodes.name: Gauge-invariant parts tilde M_0 and (tilde M')_0
nodes.statement:
Similarly we also set $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0$ and $(\tilde{{\mathcal M}}')_0$ as $(\beta_z:\;z \in H)$ invariant elements
of $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ and $(\tilde{{\mathcal M}}')$ respectively.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:

nodes.name: P need not lie in tilde M^1
nodes.statement:
We note that as a set $(\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0)'$ could be different from 
$(\tilde{{\mathcal M}}')_0$. We note also that $P\tilde{{\mathcal M}}^1P \subseteq \tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ and unless $P$ is an element 
in $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}^1$, equality is not guaranteed for a factor state $\omega$. The major problem is to show that 
$P$ is indeed an element in $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}^1$ when $\omega$ is a pure state.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:

nodes.name: F pi(tilde O_d)'' F need not be an algebra
nodes.statement:
We warn here an attentive reader that in general for a factor state $\omega$, the set ${\mathcal F} \pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)'' {\mathcal F}$, which is a 
subset of ${\mathcal F} \pi({\mathcal O}_d)'{\mathcal F}$, need not be an algebra. However by commutant lifting theorem applied to dilation $v_i \rightarrow S_i{\mathcal F}$, 
$\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'{\mathcal F}$ is order isomorphic to ${\mathcal M}'$ as $P={\mathcal F} {\mathcal E}$ is the support projection. Thus the von-Neumann sub-algebra generated 
by the elements ${\mathcal F}\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''{\mathcal F}$ is order isomorphic to $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$. However 
$\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0$ may properly include $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_{00}=\{ P\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)P \}''$ 
( as an example take $\psi$ to be the unique KMS state on ${\mathcal O}_d$ and $\omega$ be the unique trace on ${\mathcal B}$ 
for which we get $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_{00} = \mathbb{C}$ and $P\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''P$ is the linear span of 
$\{\tilde{v}_J^*,\;I,\;\tilde{v}_J:|J| < \infty \}$.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
nodes.statement_short: For a factor state the compression F pi(tilde O_d)'' F need not be an algebra; tilde M_0 may strictly contain the UHF corner (unique trace example).

nodes.name: Takesaki route to M' = tilde M is not available
nodes.statement:
Existence of a $\phi$ preserving normal conditional expectation $\int_{z \in H} \beta_z dz: {\mathcal M} \rightarrow {\mathcal M}_0$ by Proposition 2.5 ensures that modular operator of $\phi$ preserves ${\mathcal M}_0$ [Ta] and so does on 
$({\mathcal M}')_0$. However there is no reason to take it granted for $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0$ to be 
invariant by the modular group of $(({\mathcal M}')_0,\phi)$. By Takesaki's theorem such a property 
is true if and only if there exists a $\phi$-invariant norm one projection from $({\mathcal M}')_0$ 
onto $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0$. In the following we avoid this tempted route.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:

nodes.name: M' = tilde M for the unique trace although P != Q
nodes.statement:
At this stage it is not clear how we can ensure existence of a normal conditional expectation from ${\mathcal M}'$ onto 
$\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ directly and so the equality ${\mathcal M}'=\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ when $\omega$ is a pure state. Further interesting point here that the equality $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}={\mathcal M}'$ 
holds when $\omega$ is the unique trace on ${\mathcal B}$ as $v^*_k=S^*_k$ and ${\mathcal J} \tilde{v}^*_k {\mathcal J} = {1 \over d} S_k$ for all $1 \le k \le d$ where $P \neq Q$ and $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)' 
\supset \pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$. In the last proposition we have also proved if $[\tilde{{\mathcal M}}\Omega]=P$ then 
${\mathcal M}'=\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$.
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:

nodes.name: Relation between P = Q and purity
nodes.statement:
Thus a natural question that arises here: how the equality $P=Q$ is related to 
purity of $\omega$?
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:

nodes.name: Theorem 3.6 (purity iff dual support condition; Haag duality)
nodes.statement:
Let $\omega$ be as in Theorem 3.5. Then the following holds:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (a) $P$ is also the support projection of $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d))''_{|}\tilde{{\mathcal H}}$ if and only if $\omega$ is pure. 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (b) If $\omega$ is pure then the following holds:   

\noindent (i) ${\mathcal M}'= \tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ where $\tilde{{\mathcal M}} = \{ P\tilde{S}_iP: 1 \le i \le d
\}''$;

\noindent (ii) $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)' = \pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$.

\noindent (iii) $\pi_{\omega}({\mathcal B}_R)' = \pi_{\omega}({\mathcal B}_L)''$;
nodes.section: 3 Dual Popescu system and pure translation invariant states:
nodes.statement_short: P is the support projection of psi for the dual Cuntz representation iff omega is pure; for pure omega, M'=tilde M, pi(O_d)'=pi(tilde O_d)'' and Haag duality holds.
assumptions: Let $\omega$ be as in Theorem 3.5.
conclusions: (a) $P$ is also the support projection of $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d))''_{|}\tilde{{\mathcal H}}$ if and only if $\omega$ is pure.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.6
nodes.statement:
First we will prove that $\omega$ is pure if $P$ is also the support projection of the state $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$, 
where $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=[\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''\Omega]$. The support projection of $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ is $\tilde{{\mathcal E}}\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ and thus we also 
have $P = \tilde{{\mathcal E}}\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ by our hypothesis. Since $\Lambda^n(P)=\Lambda^n({\mathcal E}){\mathcal F} \uparrow {\mathcal F}$ and now
$\Lambda^n(P)=\tilde{{\mathcal E}}\Lambda^n(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) \uparrow \tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ as $n \uparrow \infty$, we also have 
${\mathcal F} = \tilde{{\mathcal E}}$. Similarly we also have for each $n$, ${\mathcal E}\tilde{\Lambda}^n({\mathcal F})=\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\tilde{{\mathcal E}})\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ 
and thus taking limit we also get ${\mathcal E}=\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$.  

\vskip 1em 
So we have $P={\mathcal E} {\mathcal F}={\mathcal E} \tilde{{\mathcal E}}=Q$. $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}=P\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''P$ is cyclic in ${\mathcal K}$ i.e. 
$[\tilde{{\mathcal M}}\Omega]=[P\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''P\Omega]= P\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=P{\mathcal E}=P$ as $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}={\mathcal E}$.  

\vskip 1em 
However $\bigcap_{n \rightarrow \infty} \tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)) = \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'' \bigcap \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'$ ( for a proof which is a simple 
application of Cuntz relation, we refer to section 5 of [Mo2]). Further $\psi$ being a factor state in $K_{\omega'}$, by Proposition 3.2 $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ is a factor. 
In particular we have $\bigcap_{n \rightarrow \infty} \tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d))\tilde{{\mathcal F}} = \mathbb{C} \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. Thus by Proposition 1.1 in [Ar2] we conclude that $||\Psi \circ \tilde{\tau}_n -\phi|| \rightarrow 0$ 
as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for all normal state $\Psi$ on $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0$ where $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0=P \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''P$ as $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}={\mathcal E}$ and support projection of $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ 
is $\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ and $P={\mathcal E}\tilde{{\mathcal E}}{\mathcal E}$. 

\vskip 1em 
Note that $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0 \subseteq {\mathcal M}_0'$ where ${\mathcal M}_0=P\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)''P$. Further by Proposition 2.5 
${\mathcal M}_0 = \{x \in {\mathcal M}:\beta_z(x)=x;z \in H \}\;\;\;$ and  $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0=\{x \in \tilde{{\mathcal M}}:
\beta_z(x)=x;z \in H \}$. Once we set $P_0=[{\mathcal M}_0\Omega]$ then we also have $P_0=[\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0\Omega]$ 
as $[\tilde{{\mathcal M}}\Omega]=P=[{\mathcal M}\Omega]$ by expending $u_z=\sum_{k \in \hat{H}} z^kP_k$ where $z \rightarrow u_z=
PU_zP$ is a unitary representation of group $H$.      

\vskip 1em
For $x \in \tilde{{\mathcal M}}, y \in \tilde{{\mathcal M}}'$ we have  
$$\phi(\tilde{\tau}(x)y)=\sum_k <\tilde{v}^*_k\Omega,x\tilde{v}^*_ky\Omega> = \sum_k <v^*_k\Omega,x y \tilde{v}^*_k\Omega>$$  
(as $v_k^*\Omega=\tilde{v}^*_k\Omega$ )
$$=\sum_k <\Omega, x v_kyv_k^* \Omega>=\phi(x \tau(y))$$
The dual group of $(\tilde{{\mathcal M}},\tilde{\tau},\phi)$ is given on the commutant by 
$(\tilde{{\mathcal M}}',\tau,\phi)$ where $\tau(x)=\sum_k v_k x v_k^*$ for $x \in \tilde{{\mathcal M}}'$. 
where commutant is taken in ${\mathcal B}({\mathcal K})$. 
Now moving to $\{\beta_z: z \in H \}$ invariant elements in the duality relation above, we verify that 
adjoint Markov map of $(\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0,\tilde{\tau},\phi)$ is given by 
$(\tilde{{\mathcal M}}'_0,\tau,\phi)$ where $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}'_0$, the commutant of $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0$ 
is taken in ${\mathcal B}({\mathcal K}_0)$ and ${\mathcal K}_0$ is the Hilbert subspace $P_0$ with $\Omega$ as
cyclic and separating vector for $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0$ in ${\mathcal K}_0$. Thus by Theorem 2.4 in [Mo3], 
there exists a sequence of elements $y_n \in \tilde{{\mathcal M}}'_0$ such that for each $m \ge 1$, 
$y_{m+n}\tau_n(y) \rightarrow \phi(y)1$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for all $y \in \tilde{{\mathcal M}}'_0 \subseteq {\mathcal B}({\mathcal K}_0)$. 
Thus $\omega$ is pure by Proposition 3.5 (e) once we recall ${\mathcal M}'=\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ as $P=Q$ 
( and so ${\mathcal M}'_0 = \tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0$ ) by Proposition 3.5 (d). This completes the proof of
 purity property of $\omega$. 


\vskip 1em  
In the following we now prove the hardest part of the theorem namely $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}={\mathcal E}$ and ${\mathcal F}=\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ if $\omega$ is pure. Proof uses extensively 
the general theory of quasi-equivalent representation of a $C^*$ algebra and we refer [BR1, Chapter 2.4.4] as a general reference.   

\vskip 1em 
We set unitary operator $V=\sum_k S_k\tilde{S}^*_k$. That $V$ is a unitary operator follows by Cuntz's relations and commuting property 
of $(S_i)$ and $(\tilde{S}_i)$. Further a simple computation shows that $V\pi(x)V^*=\pi(\theta(x))$ for all $x \in {\mathcal B} = {\mathcal B}_L \otimes {\mathcal B}_R$, 
identified with $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ and $\theta$ is the right shift. We also have    
\begin{equation} 
\theta({\mathcal E})=V {\mathcal E} V^*= \sum_{k,k'}S_k\tilde{S}^*_k {\mathcal E} S^*_{k'}\tilde{S}_{k'}=\Lambda({\mathcal E}) \ge {\mathcal E}
\end{equation} 
Similarly we also have
\begin{equation} 
\theta(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\mathcal F}} 
\end{equation}
So in particular we have $V(I-{\mathcal E})V^* \le I-{\mathcal E}$, i.e. $(I-{\mathcal E})V^*{\mathcal E}=0$.  
Also for any $X \in \pi({\mathcal O}_d)'$ we have $V^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}}X\Omega = 
\tilde{{\mathcal F}} \sum_k \tilde{S}_k X \tilde{S}_k^*\Omega$ as $S_k^*\Omega 
=\tilde{S}_k^*\Omega$. Thus $(I-\tilde{{\mathcal F}})V^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=0$ i.e. 
$V\tilde{{\mathcal F}}V^*=\Lambda(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. Similarly we also 
have 
\begin{equation} 
\theta^{-1}(\tilde{{\mathcal E}})=V^*\tilde{{\mathcal E}}V \ge \tilde{{\mathcal E}}\;\mbox{and}\; V^* {\mathcal F} V \ge {\mathcal F}
\end{equation} 
We also set two family of increasing projections for all natural numbers $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ as follows 
\begin{equation} 
{\mathcal E}_n=V^n {\mathcal E} (V^n)^*,\;\;\tilde{{\mathcal F}}_n=V^n\tilde{{\mathcal F}}(V^n)^*
\end{equation}

\vskip 1em 
Since $\beta_z(V)=V$ for all $z \in H$, $V \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ by Proposition 3.4 as $\omega$ is pure. $\omega$ being also a factor state, we have $<f,V^ng> \rightarrow <f,\Omega><\Omega,g>$ as $n \rightarrow + \mbox{or} - \infty$ for any $f,g \in \pi({\mathcal B}_{loc})\Omega$ by Power's criteria [Pow] given in (1). Since such vectors are dense in the Hilbert space topology and the family $\{V^n:n \ge 1\}$ is uniformly bounded, we get $V^n \rightarrow |\Omega><\Omega|$ in weak operator topology as $n \rightarrow + \mbox{or} - \infty$.   

\vskip 1em 
For the time being we assume that $H$ is trivial. Otherwise the argument that follows here we can use for the representation $\pi_0$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ i.e. $\pi$ restricted to $[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)\Omega]$. 

\vskip 1em 
We have following distinct cases: 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Case 1.} ${\mathcal E} \neq I \;( \tilde{{\mathcal E}} \neq I)$. Let ${\mathcal E}_n \rightarrow {\mathcal E}_{-\infty}$ as $n \rightarrow -\infty$ and thus $V{\mathcal E}_{-\infty}V^*={\mathcal E}_{-\infty}$. We claim that either ${\mathcal E}_{-\infty} = |\Omega><\Omega|$ or ${\mathcal E}_{-\infty}$ is a proper infinite dimensional projection i.e. if ${\mathcal E}_{- \infty}$ is a finite projection then ${\mathcal E}_{- \infty}=|\Omega><\Omega|$. Suppose not then the finite subspace is shift invariant. In particular there exists a unit  vector $f$ orthogonal to $\Omega$ such that $Vf=zf$ for some $z \in S^1$ and this contradicts weak mixing property i.e. $V^n \rightarrow |\Omega><\Omega|$ in weak operator topology proved above as point spectrum of $V$ has only $1$ with spectral multiplicity $1$. 

\vskip 1em 
If ${\mathcal E}_{-\infty}$ is infinite dimensional we can get a unitary operator $U_0$ from 
$F_0=\tilde{{\mathcal H}} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} {\mathcal H}$ onto ${\mathcal E}_{- \infty}$ and 
via the unitary map we can get a sequence of increasing projections $U_0{\mathcal E}_nU^*_0$ in ${\mathcal E}_{- \infty}$ and note that $U_0{\mathcal E}_nU_0^*=V^nU_0 {\mathcal E} U_0^*(V^n)^*$. Note that if ${\mathcal E}_{- \infty}$ is infinite dimension the process will not stop in finite step. Thus we have $F_0 \ominus \Omega = \oplus_{1 \le k \le n_{{\mathcal E}}} F(k)$ where the index set is either singleton or infinity and each $F(k)$ will give a system of imprimitivity with respect to $V$, where $F(1)
=F_0-{\mathcal E}_{-\infty}$. Further $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d$ being a simple $C^*$-algebra, each such imprimitivity system 
is of Mackey index $\aleph_0$ [Mo3,section 4]: We fix a nonzero $f \in {\mathcal E}-\theta^{-1}({\mathcal E}) \neq 0$ otherwise ${\mathcal E}=I$ as $\theta^n({\mathcal E}) \uparrow I$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. $\pi_f:x \rightarrow \theta^{-1}(x)f$ gives a representation of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d={\mathcal B}_L$ and we check that $[\pi_f(\theta^{-1}({\mathcal B}_L)''f] \le {\mathcal E}-\theta^{-1}({\mathcal E})$ 
as $f \perp [\theta^{-1}(\pi({\mathcal B}_R)')\Omega] \ge [\theta^{-1}(\pi({\mathcal B}_L))\Omega]$. Thus simplicity 
ensures that ${\mathcal E} - \theta^{-1}({\mathcal E})$ is a projection of dimension $\aleph_0$. Further $n_{\mathcal E}$ is either $1$
or $\aleph_0$ since $F_0$ is separable.   

\vskip 1em 
Since $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ is also a proper projection, same argument is valid for $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ with $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}_{-\infty}=
\mbox{lim}_{n \rightarrow -\infty} \theta^n(\tilde{{\mathcal F}})$ i.e. we can write $F_0 \ominus \Omega = \oplus_{1 \le k \le n_{\tilde{{\mathcal F}}}} \tilde{H}(k)$, where each $\tilde{H}(k)$ give rises to a system of imprimitivity with respect to $V$ where each system of imprimitivity is of Mackey index $\aleph_0$ where $\tilde{F}(1) = F_0-\tilde{{\mathcal F}}_{-\infty}$ 
and $n_{\tilde{{\mathcal F}}}$ is either $1$ or $\aleph_0$.        

\vskip 1em 
In the following we use temporary notation $H$ for Hilbert subspace $F_0$. For a cardinal number $n$, we 
amplify a representation $\pi:{\mathcal B} \rightarrow {\mathcal B}(H)$ of the $C^*$ algebra ${\mathcal B}$ to $n$ fold direct sum 
$n\pi=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n } \pi_k $ acting on $nH=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n } H_k$  defining by 
$$n\pi(x) (\oplus \zeta_k) = \oplus (\pi(x)\zeta_k)$$ 
where $\pi_k = \pi$ is the representation of ${\mathcal B}=\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d$ 
on $H_k=H$ where $H =[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)\Omega]$. We also 
extend $\bar{\tilde{F}} = \oplus \tilde{F}_{\alpha}$, $\bar{E} = \oplus E_{\alpha}$ and $\bar{V}=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n} V_k$ respectively. We also set notation $\Omega_k=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}\delta^k_j\Omega$. 

\vskip 1em 
Thus by Mackey's theorem, there exists a cardinal number $n \in \aleph_0$ and a unitary operator $U: nH \rightarrow nH$ so that 
$\bar{V}=U\bar{V}U^*$ and $\bar{{\mathcal E}}=U\bar{\tilde{{\mathcal F}}}U^*$. We set a representation 
$\pi^U:{\mathcal B} \rightarrow {\mathcal B}(nH)$ by $\pi^U(x)= Un\pi(x)U^*$
and rewrite the above identity as 
$$\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}[\pi_k(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega_k] = \oplus_{1 \le k \le n}
[\pi^U_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega_k]$$
where $\pi^U_k(x)=U\pi_k(x)U^*$. Note that by our construction we 
can ensure $U\Omega_k=\Omega_k$ for all $1 \le k \le n$ as the operator 
intertwining between two imprimitivity systems are acting on the orthogonal 
subspace of the projection generated by vectors $\{\Omega_k:1 \le k \le n\}$. 

\vskip 1em 
We claim ${\mathcal E}=\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. Suppose not i.e. $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} < {\mathcal E}$. In such a case we 
have
$$\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}[\pi_k(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega_k] < \oplus_{1 \le k \le n}
[\pi^u_k(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega_k]$$
Alternatively 
$$\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}[\pi_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega_k] < \oplus_{1 \le k \le n}
[\pi^u_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega_k]$$

\vskip 1em 
Thus in principle we can repeat our construction now with $\pi^U$ and so we 
get a strict partial ordered set of quasi-equivalent representation of ${\mathcal B}$. 
In the following we now aim to employ formal set theory to bring a contradiction 
on our starting assumption that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} < {\mathcal E}$. 

\vskip 1em 
To that end we need to deal with more then one representation of ${\mathcal B}$. For the rest of the proof we reset notation $\pi_0$ for $\pi$ used for the pure representation of 
${\mathcal B}$ in $H_0 =[\pi_0({\mathcal B})\Omega_0]$ where $\Omega_0$ is the cyclic vector, the reset notation for $\Omega$. Let ${\mathcal P}$ be the collection of representation $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega)$ 
quasi-equivalent to $\pi_0:{\mathcal B} \rightarrow {\mathcal B}(H_0)$ with a shift invariant vector state $\omega(x)=<\Omega,\pi(x)\Omega>$ i.e. $\omega(\pi(\theta(x))=\omega(\pi(x))$. So there exists 
minimal cardinal numbers $n_{\pi},n_0(\pi)$ so that $n_{\pi}H_{\pi}$ is unitary equivalent to $n_0(\pi)\pi_0$. Thus for such an element $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega_{\pi})$ we can associate 
two cardinal numbers $n_{\pi}$ and $n_0(\pi)$ and without loss of generality we assume that $H_{\pi} \subseteq n_0(\pi)H_0$ and $n_{\pi}H_{\pi}=n_0(\pi)H_0.$  $\pi_0$ being a pure 
representation, any element $\pi \in {\mathcal P}$ is a type-I factor representation of ${\mathcal B}$. The interesting point here that $\displaystyle{\oplus_{\pi \in {\mathcal P} }}\pi$ is also an element in ${\mathcal P}$ 
with associated cardinal numbers $\sum_{\pi} n_{\pi}$ and $\sum_{\pi} n_0(\pi)$. We say $(\pi_1,H_{\pi_1},\Omega^1) \prec (\pi_2,H_{\pi_2},\Omega^2)$ if there exists an 
isometry $U:n_{\pi_1} H_{\pi_1} \rightarrow n_{\pi_2} H_{\pi_2}$ so that 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (C1) For each $1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} $ we have 
$U \Omega^1_{\alpha} = \Omega^2_{\alpha'}$ for some 
$1 \le \alpha' \le n_{\pi_2}$;        

\noindent (C2) $n_{\pi_2}\pi_2(x)E'_2 = U n_{\pi_1}\pi_1(x) U^* $ where ${\mathcal E}'_2 \in n_{\pi_2}\pi_2({\mathcal B})'$; 
 
\noindent (C3) $\oplus_{1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} }[\pi^{\alpha}_1(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega^1_{\alpha}] < \oplus_{1 \le 
\alpha \le n_{\pi_2}}[\pi^{\alpha}_2(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega^2_{\alpha}]E'_2$.

\vskip 1em 
In the inequality we explicitly used that both Hilbert spaces are subspaces of $nH_0$ for some possibly larger cardinal 
number $n$. That the partial order is non-reflexive follows as $(\pi,H,\Omega) \prec (\pi,H,\Omega)$ contradicts 
(C3) as $I=E_2'$. Partial order property follows easily. If $\pi_1 \prec \pi_2$ and $\pi_2 \prec \pi_3$ then $\pi_1 \prec \pi_3$. 
If $U_{12}$ and $U_{23}$ are isometric operators that satisfies (C1)-(C3) respectively, then $U_{13}=U_{23}U_{12}$ will 
do the job for $\pi_1$ and $\pi_3$. Thus $\pi^U \in {\mathcal P}$ and by our starting assumption that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} \neq {\mathcal E}$ we also 
check that $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$. Thus going via the isomorphism we also check that for a given element $\pi \in {\mathcal P}$ there exists 
an element $\pi' \in {\mathcal P}$ so that $\pi \prec \pi'$. Thus ${\mathcal P}_0$ is a non empty set and has at least one infinite chain containing $\pi_0$.
 
\vskip 1em 
However by Hausdorff maximality theorem there exists a non-empty maximal totally ordered subset ${\mathcal P}_0$ of ${\mathcal P}$ 
containing $\pi_0$. We claim that $\pi_{max} = \oplus_{\pi \in {\mathcal P}_0} \pi$ on $H_{\pi_{max}}=\oplus_{\pi \in {\mathcal P}_0} H_{\pi} $ is an upper bound in ${\mathcal P}_0$. That $\pi_{max} \in {\mathcal P}$ is obvious. Further given an element $(H_{\pi_1},\pi_1,\Omega_1) \in {\mathcal P}_0$ there exists an element $(H_{\pi_2},\pi_2,\Omega_2) \in {\mathcal P}_0$ so that $\pi_1 \prec \pi_2$ by our starting remark as $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$. By extending isometry $U_{12}$ to an isometry from $H_{\pi_1} \rightarrow n_{\pi_{max}} H_{\pi_{max}}$ trivially we get the required isometry that satisfies (C1),(C2) and (C3) where cardinal numbers $n_{\pi_{max}} = \sum_{\pi \in {\mathcal P}_0} n_{\pi} \in \aleph$. Thus by maximal property of ${\mathcal P}_0$ we have $\pi_{max} \in {\mathcal P}_0$. This brings a contradiction as by our construction $(\pi_{max},H_{\pi_{max}},\Omega) \prec (\pi_{max},H_{\pi_{max}},\Omega)$ as $\pi_{max} \in {\mathcal P}_0$ but partial order is strict. This contradicts our starting hypothesis that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} < {\mathcal E}$. This completes the proof that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}={\mathcal E}$ when ${\mathcal E} \neq I$. By symmetry of the argument we also get ${\mathcal F}=\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ when $\tilde{{\mathcal E}} < 1$.  

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Case 2:} ${\mathcal E}=I \;(\tilde{{\mathcal E}}=I)$. We need to show $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=I\;({\mathcal F}=I)$ respectively. Suppose not and assume that both $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ is a proper non-zero projection. 

\vskip 1em 
We set projection $G$ on the closed linear span of elements in the subspaces $[\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F})\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega]$ for all $n \ge 0$. We recall that $\theta(X)=VXV^*$ 
where $V=\sum_k S_k\tilde{S}_k^*$ and $\theta^{-1}(X)=\tilde{\Lambda}(X)$ 
for $X \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. Thus we have 
$$V^*\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F})\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega$$
$$=\theta^{-n-1}({\mathcal F})V^*\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''V\Omega$$
$$=\theta^{-n-1}({\mathcal F}) \tilde{\Lambda}(\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega.$$
Thus $(1-G)V^*G=0$ i.e. $\theta(G) \ge G$. It is also clear that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} \le G$ 
as the defining sequence of subspaces of $G$ goes to precisely $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ ( recall 
that $\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F})=\tilde{\Lambda}_n({\mathcal F}) \uparrow I$ strongly as $n \uparrow \infty$ ). Once more we have 
$\theta^n(G) \ge \theta^n(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) = \Lambda^n(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow 
\infty$.  

\vskip 1em 
If $G$ is a proper projection we can follow the steps as in the case 1 to find a unitary operator 
$U:nH \rightarrow nH$ with $U\Omega_k=\Omega_k$ and $U\bar{V}U^*=\bar{V}$ so that $U\bar{G}U^*=\bar{\tilde{{\mathcal F}}}$. 
We consider the subset ${\mathcal P}_G$ of elements in ${\mathcal P}$ for which ${\mathcal E}_{\pi}=1$ and 
$\{\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F}_{\pi}):n \ge 0 \}$ commutes with $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}_{\pi}$ 
and modify the strict partial ordering by modifying (C3) as  

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (C3') $\oplus_{1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} }[\pi^{\alpha}_1(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega^1_{\alpha}] <  \oplus_{1 \le 
\alpha \le n_{\pi_2}}[\pi^{\alpha}_2(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega^2_{\alpha}]E'_2$

\noindent So we also get $\pi^U \in {\mathcal P}_G$ and $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$ and going along the same line we conclude that 
$G=\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. Thus we conclude that $G$ is either equal to $1$ or $G=\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Sub-case 1 of case 2:} If $G=I$ then ${\mathcal F} G = {\mathcal F}$ and so $[{\mathcal F}\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega]={\mathcal F}$ as $\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F}) \ge {\mathcal F}$. 
Thus $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} \ge {\mathcal F}$. So $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} \ge \tilde{\Lambda}^n({\mathcal F})$ for all $n \ge 1$ and taking limit we get $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} \ge I$ i.e. $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=I$. 
This contradicts our starting assumption that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ is a proper projection.  

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Sub-case 2 of case 2:} Now we consider the case $G=\tilde{{\mathcal F}} < I$. In such a case we have 
$(1- \tilde{{\mathcal F}})\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F})\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=0$ and so $\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F})$ commutes with $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ for all $n \ge 0$. 

\vskip 1em 
First we rule out the simplest possibility in the present situation for ${\mathcal F} \tilde{{\mathcal F}} = |\Omega><\Omega|$. If so then $\omega$ is
a Bernoulli state and a proof follows once we compute the following using the property $\Lambda(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ i.e.
$\tilde{{\mathcal F}}\pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}} = \pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ 
and commuting property of ${\mathcal F}$ with $\pi(s_i)^*$ to get some scalars $\bar{\lambda_i}$ such
that 
$$\bar{\lambda}_i= {\mathcal F}\tilde{{\mathcal F}}\pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}}{\mathcal F} = \pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}}{\mathcal F}$$
and so 
$$\omega(s_Is_J^*)=<\Omega,\pi(s_I) \pi(s_J)^*\Omega>$$
$$=<\Omega, {\mathcal F} \tilde{{\mathcal F}} \pi(s_I)\pi(s_J)^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}}{\mathcal F} \Omega>$$
$$=\lambda_I\lambda_J^*$$
The inductive limit state $\omega$ on ${\mathcal B}$, give rises to a pure state once restricted to ${\mathcal B}_R$ and thus we have 
${\mathcal E}=\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ by Haag duality when $\pi({\mathcal B}_R)''$ is a type-I factor. This contradicts our starting assumption that ${\mathcal E}=I$.   

\vskip 1em 
Now we set projection ${\mathcal F}'$ defined by 
\begin{equation} 
{\mathcal F}'={\mathcal F}-{\mathcal F}\tilde{{\mathcal F}}+|\Omega><\Omega|
\end{equation} 
and check by commuting property of $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ with ${\mathcal F}$ that 
$$ 
{\mathcal F}'\theta^{-1}({\mathcal F}'){\mathcal F}' = (I-\tilde{{\mathcal F}}){\mathcal F}\theta^{-1}({\mathcal F})(I-\theta^{-1}(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}))(I-\tilde{{\mathcal F}}){\mathcal F} 
+ |\Omega><\Omega|$$ 
$$= {\mathcal F}(I-\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) + |\Omega><\Omega|={\mathcal F}'$$ 
where we have used $\theta^{-1}({\mathcal F}) = \tilde{\Lambda}({\mathcal F}) \ge {\mathcal F},\; \theta({\mathcal F}) \le {\mathcal F}$ and  
$\theta(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) = \Lambda(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. 
Thus we get 
\begin{equation} 
\theta^{-1}({\mathcal F}') \ge {\mathcal F}'
\end{equation}                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     

\vskip 1em 
We also rule out the possibility that ${\mathcal F} \tilde{{\mathcal F}} = {\mathcal F}$. If so then ${\mathcal F} \le \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ and $\tilde{\Lambda}^n({\mathcal F}) \le 
\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) = \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. Taking limit we get $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=I$ as $\tilde{\Lambda}^n({\mathcal F}) \uparrow I$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. 
This brings a contradiction to our hypothesis.  
  
\vskip 1em 
So we have in particular ${\mathcal F}' <  {\mathcal F} \le I$ and ${\mathcal F}' - |\Omega><\Omega| \neq 0$. Now we will rule out the possibility of ${\mathcal F}=I$ under our hypothesis $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} < {\mathcal E}=I$. 
Suppose so i.e. ${\mathcal F}=I$, then $\tilde{{\mathcal E}}=I$ since $\tilde{{\mathcal E}} \ge {\mathcal F}$. Then $Q={\mathcal E} \tilde{{\mathcal E}} = {\mathcal E} = {\mathcal E} {\mathcal F}=P$. Thus by Proposition 3.5 (e) we get $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'= 
\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ and so we have in particular $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=[\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''\Omega]=[\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'\Omega]={\mathcal E}$. This contradicts our starting assumption once more that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} < {\mathcal E}=I$.    

\vskip 1em 
We also have $\theta^{-1}({\mathcal F}') \ge {\mathcal F}'$ and $\theta^{-1}({\mathcal F}) \ge {\mathcal F}$. Thus we can follow the steps of Case-1 with elements ${\mathcal F}',{\mathcal F},\theta^{-1}$ replacing the role of $\tilde{{\mathcal F}},{\mathcal E},\theta$ 
to get a unitary operator $U:nH \rightarrow nH$ so that $U\bar{V}=\bar{V}U$ and $U\bar{{\mathcal F}}U^*=\bar{{\mathcal F}'}$ for a 
cardinal number $n$.    

\vskip 1em 
Now we consider a further subset ${\mathcal P}_{G'}$ of ${\mathcal P}_G$ consist of quasi-equivalent representations $\pi$ to $\pi_0$ 
of ${\mathcal B}$ where $\pi$ admits the additional property: ${\mathcal F}_{\pi} < I, {\mathcal E}_{\pi}=I$ and $\{\theta^{-n}(\tilde{{\mathcal F}_{\pi}}): n \ge 0 \}$ 
commutes with ${\mathcal F}_{\pi}$ with the strict partial ordering $({\mathcal H}_{\pi_1},\pi_1,\Omega_{\pi_1}) \prec ({\mathcal H}_{\pi_2},\pi_2,\Omega_{\pi_2})$ 
given by modifying condition (C3') as

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (C3'') $\oplus_{1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} }[\pi^{\alpha}_1(\mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega^1_{\alpha}] >  \oplus_{1 \le 
\alpha \le n_{\pi_2}}[\pi^{\alpha}_2(\mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega^2_{\alpha}]E'_2$

\vskip 1em 
Since $\pi^U$ also satisfies the conditions that of $\pi_0 \in {\mathcal P}_{G'}$ by covariance relation 
of $U$ with respect to shifts once more we get $\pi^U \in {\mathcal P}_{G'}$ and $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$. Thus we can 
repeat the process and so ${\mathcal P}_{G'}$ has at least one infinite chain of totally ordered containing $\pi_0$.   
Once more by Hausdorff maximality principle we bring a contradiction to our starting assumption 
that ${\mathcal F}' < {\mathcal F}$. In other words this brings a contradiction to our starting hypothesis 
that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ is a proper projection i.e. ${\mathcal F} < {\mathcal E}=I$. Thus we arrive at $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}={\mathcal E}$ 
when ${\mathcal E}=I$. 

\vskip 1em 
By symmetry of argument used here it also follows that ${\mathcal F}=\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ when $\tilde{{\mathcal E}}=I$. This completes the proof of 
$\tilde{{\mathcal F}}={\mathcal E},\;\; {\mathcal F} =\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ for the case when $H$ is the trivial closed subgroup of $S^1$. 

\vskip 1em 
Now we will remove the assumption that $H$ is trivial using Proposition 3.4. Let $(H,\pi_0,\Omega)$ be the GNS space of the state $\omega$ on ${\mathcal B}$. 
Let $e_0$ and $\tilde{e}_0$ be the support projections of $\omega$ in $\pi_0({\mathcal B}_R)''$ and $\pi_0({\mathcal B}_L)''$ respectively. Similarly we also 
set projections ${\mathcal F}_0=[\pi_0({\mathcal A}_R)''\Omega]$ and $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}_0=[\pi_0({\mathcal B}_L)''\Omega]$. We also set projections 
$q_0=[\pi_0(\mbox{UHF})'\Omega] [\pi_0(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'\Omega]$ and $p_0=[\pi_0(\mbox{UHF})'\Omega] [\pi_0(\mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega]$.  


\vskip 1em 
$\omega$ being pure, by Theorem 3.4 any $\{\beta_z:z \in H \}$ invariant element of ${\mathcal B}(\tilde{{\mathcal H}} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} {\mathcal H})$ is an element in 
$\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. ${\mathcal E},\tilde{{\mathcal E}},{\mathcal F}, \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ are $\{\beta_z:z \in H \}$ elements. Thus once 
we identify cyclic space $[\pi_0({\mathcal B})\Omega]$ with $F_0=[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega]$, we get obvious relations 
\begin{equation} 
{\mathcal E} F_0=e_0,\tilde{{\mathcal E}}F_0=\tilde{e}_0,{\mathcal F} F_0=f_0, \tilde{{\mathcal F}}F_0=\tilde{f}_0
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation} 
P F_0 = p_0 \;\;\mbox{and} \;\; QF_0=q_0
\end{equation}
as 
${\mathcal E}=[\pi(\mbox{UHF})'\Omega]$, $\tilde{{\mathcal E}} = [\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'\Omega]$, $Q={\mathcal E}\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ and $P={\mathcal E} {\mathcal F}$. Further $V$ is also 
$\{ \beta_z:z \in H \}$ invariant and $V \pi(x)V^*=\pi(\theta(x))$ for all $x \in {\mathcal B}$ which we have identified with $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$. 

\vskip 1em 
By applying the first part of the argument with representation $\pi_0$, for pure $\omega$, we have 
$e_0=\tilde{f}_0$ and $\tilde{e}_0=f_0$ and $p_0=q_0$.  


\vskip 1em
